Background: Individuals who have experienced repeat sexual violence victimization face adverse mental and physical health outcomes, including immune and stress response functioning. We aim to further understand repeat sexual violence victimization to develop responsive and appropriate treatment for survivors of sexual violence. Methods: We present the immunological and contextual findings of a participant ( N = 1) who experienced repeat sexual violence victimization during her enrollment in The THRIVE Study, a prospective case–control study of women aged 14–45 years, who have experienced recent consensual vaginal penetration (“controls”) or forced vaginal penetration (“cases”). Participants complete a survey, HIV/sexually transmitted infection, and pregnancy testing, blood sampling for C-reactive protein and adrenocorticotrophic hormone, collection of cervicovaginal fluid for immunological biomarkers, and self-collection of saliva samples for cortisol measurements, across study visits (Baseline, 1, and 3 months). Results: The case study participant, aged 18 years upon enrollment, experienced sexual trauma before four of five study visits. Trends in the mental health indicators demonstrate reciprocal fluctuations in adverse mental health and resilience in accordance with revictimization and circumstantial changes. Suppressed immune biomarkers appear to correlate with increased adverse mental health, while mental health recovery trends with immunological recovery. The participant presents with dysregulated hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis diurnal profile. Conclusions: This profile illustrates the intra-individual biobehavioral impact of experience with revictimization over the course of 6 months, capturing experiences that are rarely studied either longitudinally or with the depth of the current research. The findings underscore the value of monitoring cervicovaginal immune functioning and hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis dysregulation in coordination with changes in mental health over the course of repeated sexual trauma. female genital tract immunology mental health sexual violence Division of Intramural Research, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases https://doi.org/10.13039/100006492 R01AI128803 center for aids research, university of california, san diego https://doi.org/10.13039/100008673 P30AI036214 district of columbia developmental center for aids research https://doi.org/10.13039/100007815 P30AI117970 cover-date January-December 2021 typesetter ts1 Introduction Women in the United States (U.S.) continue to experience a high burden of sexual violence, with profound consequences for health and wellbeing. Approximately 20% of U.S. women experience rape, defined as “any completed or attempted unwanted vaginal (for women), oral, or anal penetration through the use of physical force (such as being pinned or held down, or by the use of violence) or threats to physically harm,” 1 while 44% experience any sexual violence (SV), including sexual coercion or unwanted sexual contact. 2 Community-based samples report an even higher prevalence, particularly for women of color. 3 Young women face the highest burden of SV with 79% of rape experiences occurring before the age of 25. 2 Furthermore, two-thirds of survivors of SV experience revictimization. 4 SV impacts survivors throughout their lifespan, with physical impacts lasting for years, 5 and stress from trauma causing morbidity long-term. 6 Numerous studies have documented the behavioral links between SV and HIV acquisition among women. 7 However, the biological mechanisms are less understood. Hypotheses include disruption of the cervicovaginal epithelium leading to immune activation and inflammation, and dysregulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, impacting innate and adaptive immune responses in the female genital tract. 8 Among adolescents, cervical ectopy, inflammation, comorbid sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and maturational changes in reproductive hormone regulation may increase HIV susceptibility. 9 In addition, downstream effects of chronic stress 7 may moderate immune responses and wound healing. 7 , 10 Advancing our understanding of these complex biobehavioral pathways is essential for efforts to develop robust HIV prevention for women exposed to SV. Engaging survivors of acute SV in research is challenging. 11 Identification and recruitment of recent survivors is difficult due to limited reporting and service seeking. Survivors may perceive high participant burden, particularly with research that is longitudinal, focuses on recent SV, or involves physical examinations. Although engagement of survivors in research is acceptable even acutely post-violence, researchers must be aware of the possibility of re-traumatization and/or stigmatization of experiences, 12 and the discomfort some survivors experience during participation. 11 It is at this apex that biobehavioral research on SV and HIV sits, wherein participants must agree to (1) discuss their experience of SV that allows capture of contextual factors on risk behavior mechanisms, (2) consent to a physical examination and biospecimen collection that contributes to understanding of the physiological alterations to the systemic and local immune responses, and (3) be enrolled acutely in these biobehavioral processes. This report presents a case study of a single participant enrolled in The THRIVE Study. This case provides a contextual profile of acute SV, repeat SV, mental health, systemic and genital inflammation, and stress response outcomes 2 months post-SV. The nature of the circumstances and the multilevel assessments represent novel observations and contribute to the literature related to immune and stress responses to SV.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Sexual violence (SV) revictimization, chronic stress/trauma, and associated female genital tract injury/trauma.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Sexual violence (SV) can disrupt the cervicovaginal epithelium, leading to immune activation and inflammation, and dysregulate the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, thereby impacting innate and adaptive immune responses in the female genital tract. Chronic stress from trauma can also moderate immune responses and wound healing. The healing process of the genital tract is tightly regulated, and dysregulation can result in chronic non-healing wounds, increasing susceptibility to HIV and other STIs. Mental health indicators, such as depression, perceived stress, and experiences with battering, fluctuate in response to acute victimization events and contextual factors. Attenuated HPA axis activity, a neuroendocrine consequence of intense chronic stress and trauma, contributes to allostatic load and has downstream physiological consequences. Suppressed genital tract immunity correlates with adverse mental health (increased stress, battering, depression), potentially leading to higher susceptibility to infection and poor general immune responsiveness. Conversely, immune recovery correlates with improved mental health (lower stress, depression, increased resiliency). These findings highlight the responsive and related nature of mental health and cervicovaginal immune functioning, considering HPA axis dysregulation, and their implications for systemic immune health and HIV susceptibility.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study longitudinally investigated the intra-individual biobehavioral impacts of repeat sexual trauma/revictimization over 6 months, with the participant experiencing revictimization prior to four out of five study visits. Biomarker trends, including cervicovaginal lavage and HPA axis activity, consistently varied with the temporal proximity to victimization and environmental context. Acute victimization and chronic stress correlated with attenuated HPA axis activity and suppressed genital tract immunity (M1, M3), coinciding with increased adverse mental health indicators (stress, battering, depression). Conversely, immune and mental health recovery (M4, M5, M6) were observed during periods of greater time between victimization, removal from violent environments, or safe relationships, even after recent revictimization, indicating a direct and responsive relationship between current stress/trauma levels, contextual factors, and biobehavioral responses.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The study specifically focused on physiological alterations, particularly cervicovaginal immune responses and HPA axis dysregulation in the female genital tract, in response to vaginal rape. It highlighted that improvements in mental health and immune recovery were specifically associated with positive contextual changes, such as removal from violent environments and safe relationships, rather than merely the absence of acute victimization. For instance, CRP levels were lower than anticipated for cumulative trauma, and immune measurements were distinctly different between M3 (suppression with adverse mental health) and M5 (recovery with improved mental health) despite prior revictimization, indicating a specificity of biobehavioral responses to ongoing mental health and environmental factors rather than just the acute traumatic event itself.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The study's target population is women aged 14-45 years who have experienced nonconsensual vaginal penetration, focusing particularly on acute repeat sexual violence victimization. The primary findings are derived from a single 18-year-old White adolescent female participant from San Diego County, who experienced repeat vaginal rape. This individual represents a difficult-to-access population facing extreme circumstances and at risk for HIV susceptibility. The findings are explicitly stated as not generalizable to individuals with differing contexts.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Repeat sexual violence victimization leads to profound adverse mental and physical health outcomes, including long-term immune and stress response dysfunctions, and chronic morbidity. Specific implications include attenuated HPA axis activity contributing to allostatic load, genital tract immune suppression, increased susceptibility to HIV and other STIs due to non-healing wounds, and heightened risk for severe mental health issues like suicidal behaviors. The findings underscore the critical importance of monitoring cervicovaginal immune functioning, HPA axis dysregulation, and mental health, highlighting that contextual factors like safe environments and supportive relationships are vital for mitigating adverse effects and facilitating recovery. This necessitates a holistic and trauma-informed approach to care, particularly for HIV prevention in survivors of sexual violence, recognizing the significant impact of biobehavioral factors and individual context on health outcomes.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The findings indicate a high adverse risk associated with repeat sexual violence, encompassing attenuated HPA axis activity, chronic immunosuppression, increased susceptibility to HIV and other STIs, and severe adverse mental health outcomes. There is significant diagnostic utility in continuously monitoring cervicovaginal immune functioning, HPA axis dysregulation, and mental health indicators to understand and address the biobehavioral impacts of sexual violence, especially for HIV prevention. Additionally, the study identifies a protective benefit derived from recovery time, safe environments, and supportive relationships, which can mitigate adverse mental health effects and facilitate recovery.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The reliability and generalizability of the findings are explicitly limited as they are based on a single White adolescent female participant and should not be applied to individuals with differing contexts or without adequate comparison. The study also did not differentiate between types of nonconsensual vaginal penetration (e.g., physical force vs. threats), which could lead to different trauma manifestations and immunological consequences, further limiting the ability to discuss divergent profiles. Despite these limitations, the study underscores the value of longitudinally monitoring cervicovaginal immune functioning and HPA axis dysregulation in coordination with mental health changes during repeated sexual trauma, recognizing the need to account for menstrual cycle effects on genital immune biomarkers.
